text: María Corazón "Cory" Sumulong Cojuangco-Aquino (Tagalog: [kɔɾaˈsɔn kɔˈhwaŋkɔ aˈkino]; January 25, 1933 – August 1, 2009) was the 11th president of the Philippines, serving from 1986 to 1992 and becoming the first female president in Philippine history. She was the most prominent figure of the 1986 People Power Revolution, which ended Ferdinand Marcos's two-decade rule and established the current democratic Fifth Philippine Republic. Regarded by media outlets as the "Mother of Democracy," Aquino was married to Senator Benigno Aquino Jr., a leading critic of Marcos. The couple had five children: Maria Elena ("Ballsy"; born 1955), Aurora Corazon ("Pinky"; born 1957), Benigno Simeon III ("Noynoy"; 1960–2021), Victoria Elisa ("Viel"; born 1961), and Kristina Bernadette ("Kris"; born 1971). After her husband's assassination on August 21, 1983, she emerged as leader of the opposition against Marcos. In late 1985, Marcos called for a snap election scheduled for February 7, 1986, which was marred by massive electoral fraud, violence, intimidation, and disenfranchisement. The Batasang Pambansa declared Marcos the winner on February 15, 1986, but NAMFREL's count showed Aquino had won. Aquino called for a rally known as "Tagumpay ng Bayan" on February 22, 1986, which drew around two million people to Rizal Park. Disgruntled military officers, led by Defense Minister Juan Ponce Enrile and General Fidel V. Ramos, defected from the Marcos government and set up operations in Camp Aguinaldo and Camp Crame. Cardinal Sin mobilized public support through a broadcast on Radyo Veritas, and Aquino, who was meditating in Cebu, flew back to Manila to prepare for the takeover. On February 25, 1986, Aquino was sworn in as president, while Marcos held a separate inauguration and later fled to Hawaii. Her presidency marked the end of authoritarian rule. On February 25, 1986, Aquino issued Proclamation No. 1, calling for all officials appointed by Marcos to resign, including all 15 Supreme Court members, who then submitted their resignations. On March 25, 1986, she issued Proclamation No. 3, abolishing the 1973 Constitution and issuing the provisional 1986 Freedom Constitution, pending ratification. The reorganized Supreme Court affirmed the Aquino government as a "de jure" government in the case Lawyers League v. President Aquino. Aquino appointed all 48 members of the 1986 Constitutional Commission, led by Cecilia Muñoz-Palma, which completed its draft in October 1986. The Constitution was ratified by nationwide plebiscite on February 2, 1987, and remains in effect today. It established a bill of rights and a three-branch government, restored the bicameral Congress, and re-established the legislative branch. Elections for senators, House of Representatives, and local officials followed in May 1987, January 1988, and May 1987, respectively. During her administration, Aquino enacted landmark laws including the Family Code of 1987, the Administrative Code of 1987, and the 1991 Local Government Code, which devolved powers to local government units and allowed them to enact local taxes and share in national revenue. Economic laws such as the Built-Operate-Transfer Law, Foreign Investments Act, and the Consumer Protection and Welfare Act were also passed. The economy grew at an average rate of 3.4% from 1986 to 1992, with a positive growth in the first year and a 0.4% decline in 1991 due to the 1989 coup attempt. Inflation, which averaged 20.9% during the last six years of Marcos's rule and peaked at 50.3% in 1984, dropped to an average of 9.2% from 1986 to 1992, though it peaked at 18.1% in 1991 due to panic buying during the Gulf War. Aquino is recognized as the first female president in Asia and the only president of the Philippines to have never held any prior political office. She was diagnosed with colorectal cancer in 2008 and died in 2009. Her funeral received global media coverage, and public landmarks and monuments were named in her honor. Born on January 25, 1933, in Paniqui, Tarlac, she was the daughter of José Cojuangco, a Tarlac businessman and former congressman, and Demetria Sumulong, a pharmacist. Her father's grandfather, Melecio Cojuangco, was a member of the Malolos Congress, and her mother belonged to the politically influential Sumulong family, which included Juan Sumulong, who ran against Commonwealth President Manuel L. Quezon in 1941, and Senator Lorenzo Sumulong, who was later appointed by Aquino to the Constitutional Commission. Aquino was the sixth of eight children, two of whom died in infancy; her siblings were Pedro, Josephine, Teresita, Jose Jr., and Maria Paz. She attended St. Scholastica's College in Manila, graduating as valedictorian, then transferred to Assumption Convent for high school. After moving to the United States, she attended Ravenhill Academy in Philadelphia and Notre Dame Convent School in New York City, graduating in 1949. During her high school years, she volunteered for Thomas Dewey's 1948 U.S. presidential campaign. She earned a degree in French and a minor in mathematics from the College of Mount Saint Vincent in 1953. After returning to the Philippines, she studied law at Far Eastern University in 1953 and met Benigno "Ninoy" S. Aquino Jr., with whom she married on October 11, 1954, at Our Lady of Sorrows Parish in Pasay. She initially struggled with provincial life in Concepcion, Tarlac, and later moved to a bungalow in suburban Quezon City. Throughout her life, she was a devout Roman Catholic and fluent in French, Japanese, Spanish, English, Tagalog, and Kapampangan. Ninoy Aquino, a former Nacionalista turned Liberal, became the youngest governor in 1961 and the youngest senator in 1967. During his political career, Aquino remained a housewife, raising their children and hosting political allies at their Quezon City home. She declined to appear on campaign stages, preferring to sit in the audience. Unbeknownst to many, she sold some of her inheritance to fund her husband's candidacy. As Ninoy became a leading critic of Marcos, he was among the first to be arrested after martial law was declared on September 21, 1972, and later sentenced to death. During his incarceration, Corazon stopped buying new clothes and prohibited her children from attending parties, until advised by a priest to live normally. In 1978, Ninoy ran from prison as the leader of LABAN, and Corazon campaigned for him, delivering her first political speech. In 1980, after suffering a heart attack, Marcos allowed Aquino and her family to go into exile in the United States with U.S. President Jimmy Carter's intervention for medical treatment. On August 21, 1983, Ninoy returned to the Philippines and was assassinated on the staircase leading to the tarmac of Manila International Airport, which was later renamed in his honor. Corazon returned to the Philippines a few days later and led a funeral procession that attracted over two million people. She became a figurehead of the anti-Marcos opposition and, on December 3, 1985, officially declared her candidacy for president after a petition of 1.2 million signatures was presented to her. Salvador Laurel, leader of the United Opposition (UNIDO) party, was chosen as her running mate. Marcos attacked her on her husband's alleged communist ties, claiming the election was a fight "between democracy and communism," and accused her of playing "political football" with the United States over military bases. He also made sexist remarks, such as claiming a woman's remarks should be limited to the bedroom. The election results were widely condemned by domestic and foreign entities, including the Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines and the United States Senate. Aquino rejected a power-sharing proposal by U.S. diplomat Philip Habib. The People Power Revolution, a non-violent mass demonstration from February 22 to 25, 1986, led to Marcos's ousting and Aquino's inauguration. She is regarded as the first female president in Asia and the only president to have never held prior political office.

Corazon Aquino served as president of the Philippines from 1986 to 1992, during which time the economy recorded an average annual growth of 3.8% and an overall positive rate of 3.4% from 1986 to 1992. Inflation, which had averaged 20.9% during the last six years of the Marcos administration—peaking at 50.3% in 1984—dropped to an average of 9.2% from 1986 to 1992, though it peaked at 18.1% in 1991 due to panic buying during the Gulf War. Real GDP growth declined by 0.4% in 1991 following the 1989 coup attempt by the Reform the Armed Forces Movement, which damaged international confidence and discouraged foreign investment. Aquino's first action was to establish the Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG) on February 28, 1986, to recover the multi-billion dollar ill-gotten wealth of Ferdinand Marcos. She pursued market liberalization to counter crony capitalism, targeting the sugar and coconut industries for de-monopolization. The Philippines inherited a foreign debt of $28 billion from Marcos, which had ballooned from less than $3 billion in 1970, and Aquino chose to honor all existing debts to restore the country's international credit standing. Beginning in 1986, the administration paid off $4 billion of the debt, reducing the external debt-to-GDP ratio by 20.1 percentage points from 87.9% to 67.8% by 1991, though the country acquired an additional $9 billion in debt, increasing net national debt by $5 billion over six years. Aquino championed agrarian reform as a central social policy, issuing Presidential Proclamation 131 and Executive Order 229 on July 22, 1987, and in 1988, Congress passed Republic Act No. 6657, the Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Law (CARP), which mandated land redistribution to tenant-farmers, required landowners to receive just compensation, and limited their retention to five hectares. Corporate landowners could voluntarily divest equity in favor of workers. The Supreme Court upheld CARP's constitutionality in 1989 as a "revolutionary kind of expropriation." However, Aquino faced criticism over Hacienda Luisita, a 6,453-hectare estate inherited from her father, where instead of land redistribution, she allowed a stock redistribution scheme to corporate ownership. This was later revoked in 2006 after violence erupted in 2004 over worker retrenchment, resulting in seven deaths. From 1986 to 1990, numerous coup attempts targeted the Aquino administration, including those by the Reform the Armed Forces Movement and Marcos loyalists. On January 22, 1987, the Mendiola Massacre killed 12 and injured 51 farmers during a peaceful protest demanding genuine land reform, leading to resignations of key cabinet members, including Jose W. Diokno. Vice President Doy Laurel resigned as foreign affairs secretary in September 1987, citing government anarchy and rising communist strength. Finance Minister Jaime Ongpin, who advocated for debt repayment, was dismissed in September 1987 and died by suicide in December 1987, reportedly due to cabinet infighting and lack of progress. The administration passed CARP shortly after the massacre. Aquino conducted peace talks with the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), resulting in the creation of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) in 1989 under Republic Act No. 6734, which lasted until 2019 when it was replaced by the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). The ARMM was opposed by the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), which sought secession, and peace talks with the MILF began in 1997, ending in 2014 with a peace agreement that led to BARMM. The ARMM also led to the formation of Abu Sayyaf in 1989, a terrorist group composed of radical former MNLF members, which launched attacks starting in 1995, including the 2004 bombing of the MV Superferry 14 that killed 116 people. Shortly after taking office, Aquino ordered the release of political prisoners from the Marcos era, including Jose Maria Sison and Bernabe Buscayno, which the military resisted. The preliminary peace talks with the Communist Party of the Philippines ended after the Mendiola Massacre. Several senators opposed the presence of U.S. military bases in the Philippines, calling for the closure of Subic Bay and Clark Air Base, but Aquino opposed the demand, citing lease agreements and the strategic importance of the bases. Despite public protests gathering only 100,000 to 150,000 people, Aquino eventually conceded, and by December 1991, the government notified the U.S. that the bases had to close by the end of 1992. On December 20, 1987, the MV Doña Paz sank after colliding with the MV Vector, resulting in over 4,300 deaths, described by Aquino as a "national tragedy of harrowing proportions." The 1990 Luzon earthquake, a 7.8 magnitude event, killed an estimated 1,621 people and caused massive damage. In 1991, Mount Pinatubo erupted, killing around 800 people and displacing 20,000 residents, leaving 10,000 homeless—its second-largest terrestrial eruption of the 20th century. Tropical Storm Thelma (Typhoon Uring) on November 1, 1991, caused massive flooding in Ormoc City, killing around 5,000 people, and on November 8, Aquino declared all of Leyte a disaster area. Electric blackouts of 7–12 hours became common in Manila, costing businesses nearly $800 million by June 1992. Aquino's decision to deactivate the Bataan Nuclear Power Plant (BNPP), built during the Marcos era, worsened the power crisis, as its 620 megawatt capacity could have covered the shortfall. Critics argued the plant was unsafe and had been constructed with millions in bribes to Marcos. The administration failed to provide a viable replacement, and by the end of her term in 1992, the country faced a severe power shortage. The 1987 Constitution limited the president to a single six-year term, and although Aquino was not inaugurated under it, advisers believed she was eligible for re-election in 1992. She declined, believing the presidency was not a lifetime position. Initially, she supported Ramon V. Mitra, but later backed General Fidel V. Ramos, her defense secretary and key figure in the EDSA Revolution, who had supported her during coup attempts. Her shift drew criticism from liberal and social democratic groups and the Catholic Church, which questioned her support for a Protestant. Ramos won the 1992 election with 23.58% of the vote in a wide-open race. On June 30, 1992, Aquino formally handed over power to Ramos, leaving the inauguration ceremony in a simple white Toyota Crown to emphasize her return to ordinary citizenship. After retiring, Aquino remained politically active, opposing constitutional amendments in 1997 and 1999 that sought to remove presidential term limits, both times alongside Cardinal Jaime Sin. In 1998, she endorsed Alfredo Lim, who lost to Joseph Estrada. In 2000, she supported calls for Estrada to resign amid corruption allegations, and during the Second EDSA Revolution, she backed Vice President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo. Estrada was impeached by the House of Representatives in November 2000, acquitted by the Senate in December, and later found guilty of plunder in 2007, sentenced to reclusion perpetua with disqualification and forfeiture of ill-gotten wealth, though pardoned by Arroyo in October 2007. In 2005, after revelations of election rigging in 2004, Aquino called for Arroyo's resignation to prevent violence and political deterioration, leading to large-scale demonstrations. During the 2007 senatorial elections, she campaigned for her son, Benigno "Noynoy" Aquino III, who won. Less than a year after Corazon Aquino's death in 2009, Benigno Aquino became president.

Vice President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo was enthusiastically supported in her rise to the presidency. During the 2007 trial of Joseph Estrada, Estrada was acquitted of perjury but found guilty of plunder and sentenced to reclusion perpetua, along with perpetual disqualification from public office and forfeiture of ill-gotten wealth, on September 12, 2007. Estrada was later pardoned by President Macapagal-Arroyo on October 26, 2007. In 2005, after revelations implicating President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo in rigging the 2004 presidential elections, Benigno Aquino called on Arroyo to resign to prevent violence and political instability, and led large-scale demonstrations demanding her resignation. During the 2007 senatorial elections, Aquino campaigned for her son, Benigno "Noynoy" Aquino III, who won the race. Less than a year after Corazon Aquino's death in 2009, Benigno Aquino III won the 2010 Philippine presidential election and served as the 15th president from 2010 to 2016. In December 2008, Corazon Aquino publicly regretted her role in the 2001 Second EDSA Revolution that installed Arroyo as president and apologized to former President Joseph Estrada for her part in his ousting. Her apology drew criticism from many politicians. In June 2009, two months before her death, Aquino strongly condemned the Arroyo administration's constitutional amendment plans, calling them a "shameless abuse of power." After leaving office, Aquino traveled abroad to deliver speeches on democracy, development, human rights, and women's empowerment, including a 1994 address at the UNESCO World Commission on Culture and Development in Manila urging the unconditional release of Aung San Suu Kyi. She was a member of the Council of Women World Leaders from 1996 until her death. In 1997, she attended the wake and funeral of Saint Mother Teresa of Calcutta, whom she met during a 1989 visit to Manila. In 2005, she joined the international community in mourning Pope John Paul II. In 2002, Aquino became the first woman on the Board of Governors at the Asian Institute of Management, serving until 2006. After her presidency, she engaged in charitable work, including chairing the Benigno S. Aquino Jr. Foundation from 1992 until her death, supporting the Gawad Kalinga social housing project for the poor, and helping establish the PinoyME Foundation in 2007 to provide microfinancing for the poor. She painted and donated proceeds from her art to charity, never selling her works for personal gain. On March 24, 2008, her family announced she had been diagnosed with colorectal cancer; after being told she had only three months to live, she underwent medical treatment and chemotherapy. Healing Masses were held nationwide, and in a public statement on May 13, 2008, she said her blood tests showed she was responding well to treatment, though she experienced hair loss and appetite loss. By July 2009, she was in serious condition with loss of appetite and was confined to Makati Medical Center; her family later decided to stop chemotherapy and medical interventions. Aquino died at 3:18 a.m. on August 1, 2009, due to cardiorespiratory arrest at age 76. On the day of her death, President Arroyo declared a 10-day mourning period and issued Administrative Order No. 269 for a state funeral. Arroyo, who was on a state visit to the United States, returned to the Philippines on August 5 to pay her last respects. Aquino's children declined her offer of a state funeral. All churches in the Philippines held requiem masses, government offices flew the flag at half-mast, and her body was laid in repose at La Salle Green Hills in Mandaluyong. On August 3, 2009, her body was transferred to the Manila Cathedral in Intramuros, where hundreds of thousands of Filipinos lined the streets to view it. The cortege passed along Ayala Avenue in Makati, stopping in front of the monument to her husband Ninoy, where mourners gathered and sang "Bayan Ko." Her casket was brought into the cathedral by mid-afternoon. All Roman Catholic dioceses held Requiem Masses. On August 4, 2009, Bongbong Marcos and Imee Marcos, children of former President Ferdinand Marcos, paid their last respects despite their family feud, and were received by Aquino's daughters María Elena, Aurora Corazon, and Victoria Elisa. A final Requiem Mass was held on August 5, 2009, with Cardinal Gaudencio Rosales, Bishop Socrates B. Villegas, and other clergymen concelebrating; Aquino's daughter Kris spoke on behalf of her family. Her flag-draped casket was escorted from the cathedral to Manila Memorial Park in Parañaque, where she was interred beside her husband in her family mausoleum. The funeral procession took over eight hours, with tens of thousands lining the route. Philippine Air Force UH-1 helicopters showered the procession with yellow confetti and ships in Manila's harbor blared their sirens. Local and international leaders expressed respect for her democratic contributions. President Arroyo, once an ally, called her a "national treasure." Former President Estrada described her as the "Philippines' most loved woman" and said the country had lost its mother and guiding voice. Despite being political foes, Aquino and Estrada had reconciled and jointly opposed Arroyo. Communist Party of the Philippines founder Jose Maria Sison said their relationship was "exceptional." Former Senate President Juan Ponce Enrile urged the public to pray for her eternal repose, and although Aquilino Pimentel Jr. expressed mixed feelings, he acknowledged the nation's debt to Aquino for rallying against dictatorship. Filipinos wore yellow shirts or held masses, and yellow ribbons were tied along major roads as a symbol of solidarity. On social media, Filipinos posted yellow ribbons. Filipino Catholics called for her canonization. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas announced support for placing Aquino on the 500-Peso banknote alongside Benigno "Ninoy" Aquino Jr., who had previously been the only one featured since 1987. Messages of sympathy were sent by national and international leaders: Pope Benedict XVI praised her courage and faith; U.S. President Barack Obama called her a model of moral leadership; U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton expressed sadness and admiration for her courage; South African President Jacob Zuma called her a leader who exemplified peaceful democratic transition; Queen Elizabeth II sent condolences; Russian President Dmitry Medvedev highlighted her role in democratic reforms and her contributions to Russian-Filipino relations; Timor-Leste President José Ramos-Horta and Wan Azizah attended the funeral. After her 2010 release from prison, Aung San Suu Kyi cited Aquino as an inspiration and expressed good wishes for her son, then-president Benigno S. Aquino III. In 2008, the musical play "Cory, the Musical" was staged at the Meralco Theater, written and directed by Nestor Torre Jr. and starring Isay Alvarez, with a libretto of 19 original songs by Lourdes Pimentel. In 1986, Aquino was named Time magazine's Woman of the Year after her peaceful accession to the presidency and the ousting of Marcos. In August 1999, she was named one of the 20 Most Influential Asians of the 20th century by Time. Time also listed her among 65 great Asian Heroes in November 2006. In 1994, she was included in a reference book as one of 100 Women Who Shaped World History. In 1996, she received the J. William Fulbright Prize for International Understanding. In 1998, she was awarded the Ramon Magsaysay Award for her role in the peaceful revolution to achieve democracy. Since her death in 2009, public landmarks and memorials have been named in her honor. In 2018, Aquino, along with her husband Ninoy Aquino and 126 others, was recognized by the Human Rights Victims Claims Board as a motu proprio victim of human rights violations under Ferdinand Marcos Sr.'s dictatorship.
